findings.what: "Heavy damping leaves no peak at all" is said of "a spring or circuit", but a series loop's current peaks at 1 ÷ √(LC) at any resistance, and the practice says so; limit it to the spring's swing or the capacitor's charge.

Six footnote markers ([^1] to [^5], with [^2] used twice) sit mostly on ideas, not on rules or values he would look up: steady plus transient, "more damping gives a smaller peak", "an overdamped spring has none". Keep two or three, such as the RLC equation and the resonance condition.
"The transient is the free ringing from the last lesson" talks about the course itself; say "the free ringing of the unpushed spring" instead.
"The rule becomes m x″ + c x′ + k x = F cos ωt, and every term is a force in newtons" is 23 words with two ideas joined by ", and"; split it into two sentences, which costs no extra words.

"So every term swings at that rate, and their sizes add like AC phasors" packs two ideas into one sentence and says the sizes add, when the phasors add and the sizes do not; write "They add like AC phasors" as its own sentence.

findings.where: Screen 12 (Bilge keels) task and why; sources
findings.what: "Bilge keels add roll damping" has no quote in research.json or in the lesson's sources. The saved USNA chapter (tools/43-web_fetch.json) lists bilge keels as a roll-damping device, so cite that line.

At 360 px about 150 px of empty space sits between the text and the arrows, because the damper arrow is never more than 64 units tall. At 3 rad/s the push's arrowhead, the damper arrow and the mass term's arrowhead also bunch together at the far left.
Neither says why the mass term points against the spring: two derivatives of a cosine give −ω² times it. Add one short sentence, and trim a word elsewhere to stay under 90.

findings.where: Screen 5 (The hill), the push-rate slider (body lines 1190-1192, 1167-1172)
findings.what: Every slider value restarts the 2.6 s run, and a dot drops only once that run ends. So a drag drops one dot, for the rate where he lets go, and building the hill takes 15 taps of + with a wait after each. Drop a dot for every rate passed, so a sweep traces the hill as the brief promised.

The hill goes at 2.83, before critical damping at 4. So damping 3 and 3.5 still ring, as lesson 6 showed, yet have no hill, and the steps never say this. Screen 8's "overdamped" framing invites the wrong rule "underdamped means a peak". Add one sentence naming critical damping at 4.

The switch relabels only the charge hill. The series resonance Dan knows, the current peaking exactly where ωL = 1 ÷ ωC, appears only in a readout and in the read sentence, and the text never names it. The brief promised the current against frequency.

The "reading a model" half is thin. Only screen 11, on units, reaches back to earlier lessons, and no puzzle substitutes an answer back or checks start and end values, though the brief promised all three across the course.
"A power must have no units": in an RC circuit an electrician reads "power" as watts; say "the number in the power" or "an exponent".
The right answer is the only option with a worked figure ("about 0.24 m"), which gives it away; drop the figure or give each option one.
Nothing says why a ship's roll resonance matters: big rolls, synchronous rolling and the risk of capsize, all in the brief. The y-axis title "roll angle" would read better as "roll swing".
"The dots trace a hill, from 0.25 m … down to 0.08 m at 4 rad/s" is 28 words; split the climb and the fall.
"The hill goes near damping 2.83" can be misread, so say "disappears". The "always" in "More damping always gives a smaller peak" adds nothing.
"Try a swing X cos(ωt − φ)" brings in φ without saying it is how far the swing lags the push.
